# The Practice of Noticing

There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just after dusk, before the sky has fully surrendered to black, when the air is neither warm nor cool but something in between — a temperature that belongs to no season. I remember standing in a parking lot somewhere in eastern Oregon years ago, watching a pair of barn owls ghost across the last gray band of light above the horizon, and thinking that I had never been more fully present in my body than I was in that moment. The asphalt beneath my shoes was still radiating heat. The smell of dry sage was unmistakable. A single light was on in the office building behind me, and through its window I could see the outline of a person sitting very still, perhaps also watching the sky, perhaps simply reading.

I tell this story not because it was extraordinary — it wasn't — but because it is the kind of moment that most people would fail to register. And yet, for whatever reason, I registered it. I let it land. And years later, I can still feel the specific quality of that light, the way it made everything seem like a painting that hadn't yet dried.

What does it mean to notice things?

It sounds like such a simple question that most of us would wave it away without a second thought. Of course we notice things. We notice when we're hungry, when it's raining, when someone speaks our name. But the noticing I'm talking about is different. It is the noticing that happens when you have no particular agenda, when you are simply moving through the world with your eyes open and your mind — for once — not already full. It is the noticing that precedes understanding, that sits in the gap between stimulus and interpretation, that lets the world show you something you weren't looking for.

There is a reason, I think, that children are so much better at it than adults. A child walking down the sidewalk will stop to examine the crack in the concrete where a small green shoot has pushed through, and will kneel down beside it with the kind of reverence that most adults reserve for cathedrals. The child does not ask what the plant is called. The child does not wonder whether the plant is rare or common, useful or useless. The child simply marvels: *Here is a thing growing where nothing should grow, and it is alive, and it is reaching toward something I cannot see.*

As adults, we have largely lost the ability to marvel this way. We have learned to categorize rather than contemplate, to name rather than experience, to hurry past the extraordinary because we have convinced ourselves that it is ordinary. And in a sense, we are right — the world is full of miracle after miracle, so many that we would be paralyzed if we took them all in — but in a much deeper sense, we are wrong, because the moment we stop marveling, we stop *seeing*, and the world, for all its abundance, becomes a hallway we move through between destinations.

I have been thinking about this a great deal lately, because I have noticed a change in myself. Over the past few years, I have become increasingly aware of how much of my waking life is spent in a state of partial attention — scrolling through a phone while eating lunch, listening to a podcast while driving, reading half a paragraph of a book before checking a notification. My mind has become a restless room, always opening new windows and never closing them. And in this restless state, the world grows thin. It becomes a backdrop rather than a presence, a stage set rather than a landscape. I am present everywhere and truly *here* almost nowhere.

I don't think I'm alone in this. I think many of us are living in what the philosopher Simone Weil once described as a kind of "continuous attention" — but not the attention she meant. We are attentive to the continuous stream of information, but we are inattentive to the continuous stream of experience. We have confused the two, and in the confusion, we have allowed the second to atrophy while the first has expanded to fill every available space. We are drowning in stimulation and starving for actual perception.

But I want to be careful here, because there is a temptation in this line of thinking toward a kind of pastoral romanticism — the idea that life was somehow richer before screens, that our ancestors were walking through a world of unbroken wonder while we stumble through a landscape of artificial noise. This is not true, or at least not entirely true. People have always been distracted. People have always been busy, forgetful, inattentive. The monk in his cell was probably daydreaming about his bread. The farmer in his field was probably planning his errands. Distraction is not a modern invention. What is modern, perhaps, is its *scale* — the sheer volume of things competing for our limited attention, the engineering of systems designed not to inform us but to capture us, the transformation of every idle moment into a potential opportunity for engagement.

Still, I wonder whether the habit of noticing can be reclaimed. I wonder whether it is a skill, like playing an instrument or learning a language, that requires practice and patience and regular failure. I suspect it is. And I suspect that the practice begins not with adding something to our lives but with subtracting from it — with carving out small pockets of time in which we do nothing, see nothing, expect nothing, and simply let the world come to us.

There is a practice called *shinrin-yoku*, or forest bathing, that originated in Japan in the 1980s. It involves walking slowly through a forest with no goal, no destination, no intention other than to be present with the trees, the light, the sounds, the smells. Studies have shown that this practice reduces cortisol, lowers blood pressure, and improves immune function — but I think its more important effect is psychological. It teaches the body and the mind to relearn the act of paying attention. It teaches us, in other words, to notice again.

I have tried this in my own modest way. I live in a neighborhood with a few old oaks along the street, and on evenings when the light is particularly beautiful, I have taken to walking very slowly past them, trying to see each one for what it is rather than for what it represents — not "a tree," not "an oak," not "shade," but this specific, particular arrangement of bark and branch and leaf, this living architecture that has been growing, imperceptibly and relentlessly, for longer than I have been alive. When I do this — when I truly slow down and look — I find that the trees become almost unbearably beautiful. Their texture, their asymmetry, the way the bark peels in long papery sheets, the way the lower branches twist toward the street as if reaching for something — all of this becomes visible to me only when I stop expecting to see it.

And here, I think, is the key: *stopping the expectation of seeing*. We are such purposeful creatures that we tend to see only what we are looking for. This is useful, of course — it allows us to function, to navigate, to accomplish — but it also means that most of what we encounter passes through us without ever touching us. We are like nets stretched across a river, catching certain fish and letting everything else pass through. The practice of noticing, if it is a practice at all, is a way of widening the mesh of that net, of letting more of the world settle into the palm of our awareness.

I have noticed that the moments I remember most vividly from my life are almost never the ones I planned. I remember the texture of the lichen on a rock in a stream in Vermont — I can see it now, gray-green, crumbly, almost velvet — but I don't remember the name of the stream. I remember the way a stranger's laughter sounded as she told a story in a café in Lisbon — it had a particular musical quality, a rising note at the end of each phrase that made everyone at the table lean forward — but I don't remember what the story was about. I remember the particular shade of orange in the sky on a winter afternoon in Chicago, that color that only appears for a few minutes when the sun is low and the air is cold, and I remember thinking that it looked like the inside of a persimmon, and I remember that this comparison pleased me for reasons I couldn't fully articulate.

These memories are not significant in any conventional sense. No one would put them on a résumé or mention them in a biography. But they constitute, in a very real way, my sense of self — not a self defined by achievements or relationships or possessions, but a self defined by *quality of attention*. I am the person who noticed that particular orange, who heard that particular laugh, who felt that particular lichen between my fingers. Without these moments of pure, unmediated noticing, I would be a different person — perhaps more productive, certainly more efficient, but poorer in the deepest sense of the word.

And I think this is true for everyone. We are, all of us, the sum of what we have noticed. The person who walks through a garden and sees only "flowers" is having a different experience — a lesser experience, I would argue — than the person who walks through the same garden and notices the way one particular rose is slightly asymmetrical, its petals opening in an unexpected direction, as if it had been interrupted mid-bloom. Both people are in the garden. Only one of them is truly *there*.

There is a passage in Annie Dillard's book *Pilgrim at Tinker Creek* that has stayed with me for years. She writes about lying in a field at night and watching bats dip and dive around her, their echolocation clicking like tiny telegraphs in the dark. She describes the experience with a precision and a joy that is almost unbearable to read, because it makes you realize how much of the world you are walking past without seeing. The bats are there. They have been there all along. You just weren't looking.

I think about this passage often, especially when I am driving, because driving — that most mundane of activities — is when I am most likely to be physically present and mentally absent. My hands are on the wheel, my eyes are on the road, and my mind is elsewhere entirely, cycling through the day's obligations and yesterday's conversations and tomorrow's anxieties. The landscape outside the window becomes a blur — not because it is moving too fast to see, but because I am moving too fast to see it. I am a passenger in my own life, hurtling toward a destination while the world unfolds beside me in shades of green and gold and blue that I barely register.

But every now and then — and I don't know why, exactly — something breaks through. A hawk will appear, suspended in thermals above a highway overpass, turning with such effortless grace that it seems to be time itself that is rotating around it. Or the light will shift in a particular way, catching the side of a building and transforming it from gray to amber in the space of a single breath. Or a car will pass with a song playing that, for reasons I cannot explain, makes my chest tighten with a feeling that is part nostalgia and part something else, something I don't have a word for, a feeling like reaching for a glass of water and finding that it is full of light instead.

In these moments, I am fully alive. Not because anything dramatic has happened, but because I have, for an instant, stopped trying to arrive and started simply to be where I am. The distance between myself and the world collapses. I am not *looking at* the hawk; I am *in* the same moment as the hawk, sharing the same air, the same stillness, the same sky. And for that instant, I understand something that I usually only understand in retrospect: that this — this ordinary, unremarkable, completely unremarkable moment — is the whole of life. Not the milestones, not the achievements, not the narrative arc we construct around them, but *this*. This light. This sound. This breath.

I don't think I will ever master the art of noticing. I don't think anyone will. It is not a destination but a direction — a vector pointing toward a deeper engagement with the world that we approach but never quite reach. And perhaps that is for the best. Perhaps the goal is not to notice everything but to notice more than we did yesterday, to open one more window, to let one more miracle slip through the net.

There is an old Zen saying — I have seen it attributed to many different teachers, which perhaps is fitting for something so simple — that goes: *Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.* The tasks are the same. The attention is different. And in that difference — in the quality of attention brought to the most ordinary acts — lies the entire revolution of being alive.

Chop wood. Carry water. Notice the grain in the wood. Notice the way the water bends light. Notice the weight of the axe in your hand. Notice that you are holding an axe, that you have hands, that the wood is from a tree that grew in soil that was once bedrock that was once something else entirely, something so ancient that to comprehend it would be to comprehend the whole sweep of geological time — and yet here it is, here in your hands, in this ordinary moment, this one moment that you will never live again.

Notice.

That is the whole of it. Not as a moral lesson or a productivity hack or a wellness strategy, but as a simple act of respect — respect for the world, respect for time, respect for the astonishing fact that you are here at all, in this body, in this place, at this particular coordinate of light and history and breath. You are here. The world is here. And for a few brief moments each day, if you are lucky, if you slow down, if you open your eyes, you will notice.

I think that's enough. I think that has always been enough.
